nameStory: Stretch spiders get their name from their remarkably elongated bodies that look like they've been pulled like taffy. When threatened, they extend their long legs forward and backward, stretching themselves along a twig or blade of grass to become nearly invisible. The 'versicolor' part means 'various colors,' hinting at this species' ability to show up in different shades.
description: The Tetragnatha versicolor is a tiny, pencil-thin spider that's much longer than it is wide, giving it a distinctly stretched appearance. Females reach about 6.5mm long while males are slightly smaller at around 5mm - that's smaller than your pinky nail! These little orb weavers typically display warm colors ranging from dark yellow to pale orange, and despite their small size, they're skilled web builders that hunt at night.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated and narrow body that looks stretched like a hot dog, much longer than it is wide with a sleek, streamlined profile

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny spider - females about 6.5mm, males around 5mm long, roughly the size of a grain of rice but much thinner

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark yellow to pale orange coloration that may appear almost golden in sunlight, with a smooth, somewhat glossy texture

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged with a distinctive wide separation between the front and back eye rows - more spaced out than other stretch spiders

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic orb webs (circular with radiating spokes) but removes the web during day, making them hard to spot until evening

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, stretches legs forward and back to align perfectly with twigs or stems, becoming nearly invisible

habitat: Unlike most stretch spiders, this species avoids water and prefers drier environments like shrubs, trees, and garden plants away from ponds or streams. You'll find them in forests, grasslands, and suburban yards throughout New England, particularly on woody plants and bushes. They're habitat generalists, meaning they adapt well to various environments as long as they're not too wet.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin building webs in shrubs and trees. Look for their distinctive elongated silhouettes on branches during late evening hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults actively hunting and mating. Webs are most commonly seen at dawn and dusk before being taken down during daylight.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs and adults remain active until first hard frost. This is often the best time to spot them as vegetation thins out.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and eggs overwinter in protected locations like bark crevices or leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: This tiny spider is a master of disguise - when threatened, it can stretch its legs and body to perfectly mimic a twig, complete with staying motionless for over an hour until danger passes, making it nearly impossible to spot even when you're looking right at it!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other stretch spiders in the same genus, but this species is the 'dry land' specialist - if you find a stretch spider away from water sources like ponds or streams, it's probably versicolor. Memory trick: 'versicolor avoids water' - both start with 'v' and 'a'.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'long-jawed orb weavers,' these spiders don't have noticeably long jaws to the naked eye - the name refers to microscopic features that scientists use for identification. The 'orb weaver' part is more obvious since they build those classic round, spoke-wheel webs we all recognize.
compareHints: Unlike the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver that stays near water and has greenish coloring, versicolor prefers dry areas and shows yellow-orange tones. It can be distinguished from the Common Stretch Spider by its wider eye spacing and preference for staying away from aquatic environments. The key difference from all its relatives is habitat - if it's not near water, it's likely versicolor.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tetragnatha relatives, the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out with its vivid green coloration, while the Common Stretch Spider tends to be more yellowish or brownish, and the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver has distinctive metallic silver markings.
Among New England's long-jawed orbweavers, the Common Stretch Spider is distinguished by its extreme elongation and distinctive straight-line defensive posture.
Among its stretch spider relatives, the Elongate Stilt Spider has the most extreme body elongation - much more stretched than the Common Stretch Spider or Green Long-jawed Orbweaver.

Among the Tetragnatha genus in New England, the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out for its distinctive metallic silvery appearance, while the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver appears more yellow-green and the Common Stretch Spider tends to be brownish.
Compared to its relatives, the Straw-colored Stretch Spider is consistently paler than the bright green T.
Unlike the Common Stretch Spider which has a more uniform abdomen, the tailed long-jawed orbweaver has that distinctive rear projection.
